entries.title: House Republicans Ram Through Reconciliation 3.0 Despite Little Senate Buy-in
entries.summary: The framework includes money for defense, farm assistance and changes to voting laws.
entries.content:
House Republicans on Wednesday muscled through a $95 billion budget framework that includes President Donald Trump’s request to fund the Iran war, farm aid and grants for states to encourage voter ID requirements.

The resolution’s slim 216-214 passage comes after the White House and House GOP leaders for weeks worked to corral rank-and-file Republicans in support of the measure. Lawmakers voiced concerns about various components of the third package. Republican leaders are using the budget reconciliation process to get around a Democratic filibuster in the Senate.

The budget resolution includes $73 billion for defense and intelligence, $12 billion for farm assistance and $10 billion for the voter ID grant programs.

“Here we are, reconciliation 3.0, supporting our troops in their time of need … bullets and bombs to finish the job,” Rep. Jodey Arrington (R-Texas), the chair of the House Budget Committee, said on the House floor ahead of the vote. “Strengthen our food supply and ultimately, we want to safeguard the integrity of our elections.”

Before the vote, House Republicans across the ideological spectrum criticized the budget resolution, some arguing that it was too narrow and some complaining it did not contain enough conservative priorities or spending cuts to offset the cost.

Speaker Mike Johnson previously pledged to lawmakers that the party’s third reconciliation bill would be a broader package. Part of the pitch from Johnson and the White House this week was that Republicans would instead shift some conservative priorities to a fourth reconciliation package — after the November midterms.

Ultimately, conservatives, moderates and fiscal hawks backed the nearly $100 billion budget blueprint that did not include offsets for the new spending. Two House Republicans, Rep. Warren Davidson of Ohio and Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, broke with their leaders and opposed the package. Independent Rep. Kevin Kiley of California also voted against it.

The vote is the opening salvo in what is expected to be an extended back-and-forth between Republicans in the House and Senate over how to pass the party’s third reconciliation package this Congress. Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters this week that he would hold the House’s budget resolution until lawmakers can sort out government funding, which is set to expire at the end of September.

The House separately approved a bill largely along party lines that would punt the government funding fight until after the midterms, funding the government into December. That plan faces an uncertain future in the Senate, where GOP leaders will need the support of at least seven Democrats to pass any government funding measure. Senate Democrats have been hesitant to vote to fund the government over the past year and a half without concessions from Republicans. Thune indicated if Senate Democrats fail to negotiate a bill to avoid a shutdown he could decide to add it to the party-line package.

House and Senate Republican leaders are working against a ticking clock to negotiate agreement on a package that can pass both chambers. Thune has repeatedly said the SAVE Act provisions, focused on Trump’s priority bill requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote, do not have the votes to pass in the Senate. House lawmakers are scheduled to leave Washington on Thursday for a monthlong August recess and return with just four more weeks in session before the November midterms. Senators are in Washington until the end of July, and will return in September with just three weeks of session left.

entries.title: Soldier Shot Near White House Files Claim Against the Secret Service
entries.summary: Benjamin Del Real Jr.’s attorney said “it's clear as day” that the U.S. Secret Service shot his client.
entries.content:
Benjamin Del Real Jr., a 25-year-old bystander who was injured during a Secret Service shootout with a suspect in May near the White House, has filed a personal-injury claim against the agency, alleging a Secret Service agent was actually the one who shot him.

“We have a very reliable and confidential source that tells us — who saw the CCTV footage of this incident — who says in no uncertain terms that the Secret Service shot Ben,” Joseph Murphy, Del Real’s attorney, said. “It's clear as day.”

Del Real and his father were visiting Washington on May 23 when the suspect, Nasire Best, opened fire on a security checkpoint near the intersection of 17th Street and Pennsylvania Avenue NW. Del Real, who is an active-duty U.S. Army soldier from Kansas, was hit by a bullet during the incident.

During the news conference announcing the lawsuit, Murphy said that the Del Real family was standing about 20 yards away from the suspected gunman, telling reporters that meant the Secret Service should have been “more surgical in their taking down of the shooter.”

Del Real’s attorneys have attempted to negotiate with the Secret Service, Murphy said, but they have not “gotten any real, definitive or substantive answers at all in terms of what occurred.” Del Real is filing a claim under the Federal Tort Claims Act, which is the first step toward suing the federal government.

“It's part of the reason why we're frustrated here, and we're seeking more answers,” Murphy told reporters. “We have given them two months. I think we've been reasonable.”

Murphy acknowledged that the U.S. Secret Service is a “highly trained and highly effective organization,” but said agents “fell well short of their training” when Del Real was shot.

The Secret Service referred questions about the claim to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Del Real was shot in the abdomen and tore his ACL during the incident, his lawyers said. Emergency services rushed Del Real to George Washington University Hospital to undergo emergency surgery where doctors removed parts of his colon and part of his small intestine. The soldier has had two surgeries since the shooting and has had to recover from an infection during his medical treatment.

“I enlisted a year and a half ago, and it's been one of the greatest journeys that I've taken thus far in my life,” Del Real told reporters when asked about returning to his role in the U.S. Army. “I am concerned with the ability to be able to perform the job that I signed up to do at this time.”

entries.title: House Lawmakers Pass Bill Restricting Congressional Stock Trading
entries.summary: But it’s likely dead on arrival in the Senate.
entries.content:
The House on Wednesday passed legislation that would prevent members of Congress, their spouses and their children from buying individual stocks.

But the bill is likely dead on arrival in the Senate, where Republican leadership has shown little interest in the matter. And some lawmakers in both chambers say the House bill does not go far enough to mitigate potential conflicts of interest between lawmakers’ official actions and their personal finances.

The Stop Insider Trading Act, which passed on a 232-198 vote with 13 Democrats joining Republicans, allows lawmakers and their immediate family members to retain, and eventually sell, individual stocks they already hold. Lawmakers would be required under the bill to publicly disclose their plans to sell stock holdings between seven and 14 days in advance of a sale.

The legislation also imposes a fine of $2,000 or 10% of a transaction — whichever is greater — for disclosure and trading violations.

House Republicans combined the measure with language from another bill that would require voters to present photo ID to cast a ballot — President Donald Trump’s top priority ahead of the midterm elections.

Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas), who has worked on several stock-ban bills this decade, said on the House floor Wednesday afternoon before the vote that he would have preferred a standalone vote on the stock-trade language. But, Roy added, he was “proud of the legislation.”

“This is a giant step forward. I wish my colleagues on this side of the aisle and my colleagues on this side of the aisle would recognize that and praise it,” Roy said.

Republican lawmakers lined up alongside Roy to express their support. Rep. Mike Lawler (R-New York) said he supported ending stock trading by members of Congress because “trust in our democracy cannot be a luxury item.”

“It must be the everyday expectation of every American,” Lawler added.

House Democrats largely opposed the bill, characterizing it as a watered-down version of other bipartisan bills that would go further by barring members of Congress and their families from owning stocks altogether and apply the same standards to the president and vice president.

“Two things can be true at the same time. I can support voter ID requirements, which I do, and I can support banning members of Congress from trading stocks, which I do,” Rep. Chrissy Houlahan (D-Pennsylvania) said during debate on the House floor Wednesday afternoon. “I can also oppose this bill because it is not in that honest attempt to do either.”

But Rep. Bryan Steil (R-Wisconsin) criticized his colleagues for making “Goldilocks arguments” claiming the bill went too far or did not go far enough.

“I believe this is our opportunity where we can simply stop members of Congress from trading individual stocks. Period. Full stop,” Steil said during remarks on the House floor. “Doing so removes even the appearance of wrongdoing. Americans should be confident that individuals working here are working on their behalf, not on behalf of their own financial interests.”

Democrats worked alongside Republicans on other stock-trade ban proposals this year, including the Restore Trust in Congress Act.

A bipartisan group of lawmakers including Roy and Reps. Seth Magaziner (D-Rhode Island), Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York), Tim Burchett (R-Tennessee), Pramila Jayapal (D-Washington) and Anna Paulina Luna (R-Florida) negotiated the Restore Trust in Congress Act for months before unveiling the legislation last September.

The bill would have barred members of Congress and their families from trading and owning individual stocks and forced them to divest from any stock holdings, allowing them to defer paying taxes on the sale if they reinvest in a mutual fund.

But unlike the Stop Insider Trading Act, the Restore Trust in Congress Act and other similar measures failed to generate enough support in the current Congress to advance to the full House for a vote.

Ethics watchdogs including Common Cause, Campaign Legal Center, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, Public Citizen and the Project on Government Oversight supported the Restore Trust in Congress Act. They expressed serious concerns about the Stop Insider Trading Act allowing lawmakers to continue to own or sell stocks.

The Senate is unlikely to take up the Stop Insider Trading Act –– the measure is not likely to overcome the Senate’s 60-vote filibuster, especially with the voter ID provisions added, and previous stock-ban bills have stalled in the upper chamber. 

A much stronger stock-ban bill championed by Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Missouri) advanced out of a Senate committee in July 2025 with the help of the committee’s Democratic members. But the bill has languished since then and Senate leadership hasn’t scheduled a vote on it.

Hawley’s bill, called the Halting Ownership and Non-Ethical Stock Transactions Act, or HONEST Act, would require members of Congress, the president and vice president, along with their spouses and dependent children, to sell their existing individual stocks and prevent them from buying new ones.

While Hawley said the Stop Insider Trading Act is “not nearly as robust as I would like,” he didn’t outright oppose it, saying something is better than nothing.

Momentum has been building for Congress to advance a stock-trading ban after a series of high-profile controversies, such as lawmakers making a flurry of stock trades immediately before and after the initial COVID-19 pandemic shutdowns of early 2020.

NOTUS and other news organizations have also identified dozens of members of Congress this decade who’ve violated the disclosure provisions of the existing Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act, or STOCK Act, of 2012.

Barring members of Congress from trading individual stocks has high public support among Republican, Democratic and independent voters alike, according to polls.

The STOCK Act of 2012 was the last major piece of legislation that regulated congressional stock trading and prohibited conflicts of interest. The bill clarified that insider-trading laws apply to Congress and expanded financial-disclosure requirements, but did not place limits on lawmakers’ ability to buy, sell and own individual stocks.

entries.title: House OKs a $1 Trillion Defense Bill in a Tight Vote
entries.summary: Democrats largely opposed the bill over the Iran war, the price tag and anti-trans language.
entries.content:
The House narrowly approved sweeping defense policy legislation that codifies President Donald Trump’s Pentagon plans, including his “Department of War” rebrand and push to deny coverage for health care to transgender troops.

Just six Democrats voted for the $1.15 trillion National Defense Authorization Act, while all but seven Republicans backed the bill. The final vote was 216-212.

The NDAA’s passage was a win for House Speaker Mike Johnson, who agreed this month to merge the SAVE America Act with the defense policy bill in order to quell a rebellion from his hard-right members, led by Florida Rep. Anna Paulina Luna. The SAVE America Act, a top priority for Trump, would require proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections and showing an ID to cast a ballot.

Democrats largely rejected the NDAA as a referendum on the Iran war and Trump’s budget request, which seeks $1.5 trillion for defense while slashing social programs.

“Whatever else may be said about the NDAA — there’s a lot of positive aspects to it — it will continue to support the Department of Defense that the president is using to wage this war, this incredibly disastrous, terrible decision of a war,” said Rep. Adam Smith of Washington, the top Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee.

The panel’s top Republican, Rep. Mike Rogers of Alabama, has argued the bill is necessary to support troops, foster innovation and strengthen an eroding defense industrial base in the face of China’s growing might.

“We are giving industry the certainty it needs to invest, expand and produce faster,” he said.

House Republicans on Tuesday crossed a red line for many Democrats when they added a provision to ban gender-affirming care for service members and their dependents through Tricare, the military’s health care plan. They also included an amendment barring transgender girls from participating in girls’ sports at Defense Department schools for military families.

Other hard-right amendments included language to approve the default when qualified service members and Pentagon civilian employees ask commanders for permission to carry personal firearms on military installations.

Lawmakers also added some measures opposing divisive Pentagon policies, including one that would restore collective bargaining at the Defense Department. Others include a mandate to restore military base names selected by Congress’ bipartisan renaming commission, new reporting requirements when senior military officers are fired and restrictions on the construction of the Navy’s proposed “Trump-class” battleship.

The bill is not in its final form. Democrats and Republicans typically reconcile separate versions from the House and Senate with final passage expected in December. The NDAA is considered must-pass legislation, and Congress has drafted and passed a version each year for decades.

The most controversial provisions in the House-passed bill have little chance of clearing the Senate, where bipartisan support is needed to advance legislation. The views of the president, who holds veto power, will also be a factor in composing any final bill.

Senate Democrats will “robustly” oppose any GOP anti-trans provisions, said Sen. Jack Reed (D-Rhode Island), the Senate Armed Services Committee’s ranking member. “I mean, getting into the medical diagnoses and all those things, it's an issue that is more to appease their supporters, not to help personnel or to make the military better.”

Last week, Senate Democrats blocked Republicans from bringing their chamber’s version of the bill to the floor to protest the Trump administration’s Iran war and attempt to gain leverage in negotiations over next year’s federal budget.

House and Senate negotiators have in the past reconciled a House-passed and Senate Armed Services Committee-passed bill. This week, Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Mississippi), the panel chair, did not rule out that strategy.

“That's not an ideal process, but we'll get it done at some point, the sooner the better,” Wicker said. “But it speaks volumes that our Democratic colleagues were not even willing to proceed to the bill.”

entries.title: Judge Sets Maduro Criminal Trial for June 2027
entries.summary: U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein noted that he would have to spend significant time privately reviewing sensitive evidence behind closed doors.
entries.content:
NEW YORK — Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro’s criminal trial in New York City will start in June 2027, a judge ruled during a Wednesday hearing, a timeline that reflects the mountain of classified evidence in a case that involves spy agencies, the U.S. military and law enforcement.

The court hearing was the ousted Venezuelan president’s first public appearance in months, as his case slowly advances. It was brief, with little discussion about the pending issues in the case.

Maduro appeared healthy and composed when he entered the courtroom at noon, sporting thick-framed glasses and a tan, short-sleeved prison uniform. He scanned the crowd in the tightly packed gallery before nodding and saying “good morning” in a firm tone. He made a tight smile beneath his signature mustache as he made his way toward his lawyers, then sat and put on black headphones to hear a translation of the proceedings.

Maduro, who remained in power after contested national elections, was captured in a U.S. military operation in Caracas in January and brought to the United States, an action he described as “kidnapping.” The DOJ charged him with multiple offenses including conspiracy to commit narco-terrorism and conspiracy to import cocaine, alleging that the South American dictator had morphed into a corrupt public official and drug kingpin.

The U.S. approach echoed the 1989 American military-led capture of Panamanian military dictator Manuel Noriega, who was convicted of drug charges and spent decades in U.S., French and Panamanian prisons before his death. Maduro, 63, and his wife, who was also seized, face potential life sentences if convicted on charges he flooded the United States with cocaine.

A major hang-up early on pertained to the Trump administration’s initial refusal to allow Maduro to tap Venezuelan public funds to pay for his defense lawyers, but the government has since relented.

Defense lawyer Barry Pollack alluded to making future arguments about Maduro being protected by sovereign immunity and limitations in the U.S. government’s jurisdiction.

U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein noted that he would have to spend significant time privately reviewing sensitive evidence behind closed doors as part of the Classified Information Procedures Act of 1980 and asked repeatedly whether the next year would be enough time for him to decide what documents and information can be used by prosecutors in open court.

“This is a realistic schedule,” Pollack said.

A defense lawyer for the ousted president’s wife, Cilia Adela Flores de Maduro, who was also in the room, concurred.

Lawyers must lay out their legal arguments in time for the next court hearing, set for Nov. 17, and the judge scheduled a final conference on May 25, a week before the trial is expected to start.

Hellerstein, 93, struggled to walk to the bench and speak during the hearing. He could oversee what could be a weeks-long trial. Prosecutors and defense lawyers made no mention in court of how long the trial could go.

Hellerstein appears to be sensitive to the optics of having a foreign leader face justice in American courts; at one point he asked an agent with the U.S. Marshals Service, who had tapped Maduro’s shoulder, to back away when Maduro began to whisper to his lawyer.

“Let them speak. Let them speak,” Hellerstein said in a hoarse voice.

When the hearing was over, Maduro stood and adjusted a second pair of reading glasses in his left chest pocket. He shook hands with defense lawyers and left the courtroom.

entries.title: Senate Farm Bill Negotiations Are Stuck During McConnell’s Absence
entries.summary: Democrats want a delay in when states must start sharing SNAP costs, and have leverage with McConnell away.
entries.content:
Sen. Mitch McConnell’s absence from the Agriculture Committee has put farm bill negotiations into a standstill.

Democrats want to delay when states must start sharing costs under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, a change Republicans put in a previous law. Committee Chair John Boozman (R-Arkansas) has wanted to keep that potential delay out of negotiations.

But with McConnell, the second-ranking Republican on the panel, away from the Senate for more than a month for medical reasons, Democrats have more leverage over the process.

The committee is currently split 11-11, making it impossible to advance legislation without bipartisan support. The stalemate over SNAP has dimmed Boozman’s hope of marking up the Senate version of the farm bill at the end of July.

Boozman acknowledged the setback without the Kentucky Republican’s presence. “We're in a situation where we are trying to get Sen. McConnell back. He's progressing well, so hopefully we'll get him back soon,” he said.

The Senate is set to leave soon for a break that lasts until mid-September, which leaves Congress with a steep challenge to pass the farm bill before the current version expires at the end of September.

The potential expiration is a pressure point on both parties, as farmers face record-high bankruptcies and surging input costs. The multi-year bill addresses an array of agricultural and food programs, and the last farm bill’s economic assumptions have largely become outdated.

Democrats have demanded a two-year delay in shifting SNAP benefit costs under last year's reconciliation law, which requires states to start covering 5% to 15% of SNAP benefit costs beginning in October 2027, based on their payment error rates. The error rate measures overpayments and underpayments to recipients, not fraud.

“We want a two-year delay on SNAP provisions,” Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois), a member of the committee, told NOTUS. “It's a deal-maker and a deal-breaker.”

Democrats point to an exception that the worst-performing states already received in last year’s negotiation process for the reconciliation bill. States with error rates of 20% or higher got a two-year delay in the law as part of a deal that secured the vote of Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) for the broader reconciliation package; Alaska's error rate is among the highest in the country.

Democrats are asking for the same delay for every state.

Boozman has acknowledged states have had more trouble than expected getting under the 6% error-rate threshold that triggers the cost share: Only nine states achieved full compliance in fiscal 2025, while the national average of the error rate was 10.62%.

Boozman said he would rather not touch SNAP in the Senate version of the farm bill, but he hasn’t ruled it out either. Other Republicans say they aren’t ready to budge.

“I think at some point they [Democrats] come to a realization that they get to keep pushing their social program, and they will,” Sen. John Hoeven (R-North Dakota), a member of the committee, told NOTUS. “We get that, but it's time to move on and get something done.”

Hoeven also noted elements of the farm bill that Democrats do heavily support, and said he thinks that going without a bill would be a bridge too far.

For now though, Democrats seem resolved not to back down from their demand.

“I think it’s too important,” Sen. Adam Schiff (D-California), a member of the committee, told NOTUS.

Schiff said farm bills are traditionally bipartisan, and this one’s pathway for consensus resides with a delay in the SNAP cost shift. “We desperately want a farm bill on both sides of the aisle. There is a path forward, but it will require some mitigation of the harm from the SNAP cuts,” he said.

Republicans say deadline pressure could be alleviated somewhat when farm-related provisions included in the reconciliation bill come online in October.

The farm bill has been overdue since the last five-year authorization, the 2018 Agriculture Improvement Act, expired in 2023. Congress has spent the years since patching it together with extensions.

entries.title: The Trump Administration Moves to Stop Collecting Workplace Demographic Data
entries.summary: Democrats say the race, sex and ethnicity data is central to enforcing antidiscrimination laws.
entries.content:
The Trump administration has moved to stop requiring companies to report demographic data, undoing a 60-year-old precedent that Democrats and civil rights experts say could make it harder to enforce antidiscrimination laws.

Republicans on the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, which is charged with enforcing civil rights laws against workplace discrimination, voted on Tuesday to end the agency’s decades-long practice of collecting race, sex and ethnicity workforce data.

The commission’s Republicans argue that these reporting requirements may actually lead to discrimination because they “may encourage employers to discriminate against employees who are not considered ‘minorities,’” the proposed rule reads.

The agency’s lone Democratic commissioner, Kalpana Kotagal, said that ending the collection of race and sex data would “kneecap the agency’s ability to investigate discrimination and protect workers.”

“These efforts should be seen for what they are: an attempt to weaken equal employment opportunity, and to undermine progress for women and historically marginalized communities,” Kotagal said in a statement.

The move to halt data collection is the latest change in an ongoing transformation of the workplace civil rights agency, which Congress created under the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

The bipartisan commission is typically composed of five presidentially-appointed members who serve five-year terms. No more than three members can be from the same party.

But early in his administration, President Donald Trump made the unprecedented move of firing two of the panel’s three Democratic commissioners, leaving only Kotagal and Republican Andrea Lucas, currently the EEOC’s chair, on the commission. Another Republican commissioner, Brittany Bull Panuccio, has since been appointed and confirmed by the Senate, giving the Republicans the majority at the EEOC, which is at its lowest staffing levels in over 45 years after about a quarter of its workforce since Trump took office.

Under Lucas, the EEOC has prioritized “remedying DEI-related race and sex discrimination.” Late last year, she posted a viral video on X asking, “Are you a white male who has experienced discrimination at work based on your race or sex?” and telling viewers that they may be able to file a claim.

In addition to claiming that the demographics data collection may promote discrimination, the EEOC is also arguing that there are also constitutional concerns that the reporting requirements may violate equal protection guarantees and that ending the reporting requirements will result in cost savings.

Kotagal, in her statement, said that the constitutional claim is “untethered from reality” and that the EEOC may now have to resort to subpoenas and requests for information to get the data from employers, processes that could wind up in expensive court battles.

Democrats have also questioned the administration’s reverse-discrimination concerns. Chai Feldblum, who was a Democratic EEOC commissioner for over eight years beginning in 2010, told NOTUS that it is an “absolutely false assumption” that employers that discover a discrepancy such as a lack of Black people in management will “necessarily violate the law” by deciding, “My next three hires will be Black people.”

“That is illegal,” said Feldblum. But “there are many legal ways to remedy a disparity.”

The data collected by the EEOC is instrumental to the agency’s enforcement capacity, said Kotagal, pointing to a $5.5 million settlement with trucking company Central Transport over allegations that the company intentionally refused to hire qualified female truck drivers as an example.

Analyzing the company’s data showed statistically significant disparities in the hiring of male drivers, which helped the EEOC find cause that there had been discrimination, Kotagal said.

Demographic data helps the EEOC put discrimination allegations into context and guide investigations, said Karla Gilbride, who previously served as EEOC general counsel after being appointed by former President Joe Biden.

“Losing this data will take an important tool out of the EEOC's law enforcement toolbox and slow down the investigative process, as the EEOC will have to request the same type of information from employers after a charge is received instead of already having it at the investigation's outset,” Gilbride told NOTUS in a statement.

The decision to halt reporting requirements, if finalized, would also affect what information employers can access to see how their workforce compares to industry norms. Currently, the EEOC publishes aggregate level summaries of the data it's moving to ax.

Even with the EEOC changing its priorities, employers could still be subject to legal challenges if they have discrimination problems, said Feldblum, noting that “the law does not change because chair Lucas wants it to change.”

The EEOC is one of many parts of the government that is moving to dismantle demographic data collection. LGBTQ+ data has especially been targeted, and data scientists fear that race and ethnicity data is becoming another target for the Trump administration, as NOTUS has previously reported.

The EEOC is collecting public comments on the proposed rule to roll back reporting requirements for 30 days and is holding a public hearing on the plan on Aug. 11.

entries.title: EPA Must Fund Environmental Grants It Illegally Canceled, Judge Rules
entries.summary: A federal judge said the agency “is defying” his previous order voiding the cuts.
entries.content:
The Environmental Protection Agency must administer the Biden-era Environmental and Climate Justice Grants it illegally canceled last year, a federal judge ordered Wednesday.

Last month, U.S. District Judge Richard Mark Gergel found that the agency’s DOGE-driven cuts to the $2.8 billion block grant program were “arbitrary and capricious and unlawful” and voided the internal guidance that ordered the terminations.

A coalition of cities and nonprofits brought the lawsuit against the EPA after it axed funding to their programs early last year. Following Gergel’s ruling last month, the coalition argued in court that the order compels the agency to restore said funds.

The EPA in turn argued the order “does not compel further action” and refused to reinstate the grants.

On Wednesday, Gergel handed the coalition a win, writing that “the EPA is defying this Court’s prior order” and clarifying that it must “comply with its statutory obligations to administer the ECJ Program through September 30, 2026” — the date through which Congress funded the programs.

The grants, which were created as part of the Inflation Reduction Act under the Biden administration, went toward programs aimed at curbing carbon emissions, reducing pollution and building climate-resistant infrastructure in underserved parts of the country.

An EPA spokesperson said the agency is “reviewing the decision.”

entries.title: Darline Graham? Republicans Don’t Know Her.
entries.summary: Graham decided to run for a full Senate term after being appointed to the seat after her brother’s death, but people are still learning what she stands for.
entries.content:
Darline Graham made it official that she wants to run for a full term to represent South Carolina in the Senate. But unlike her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died suddenly earlier this month, few people know where she stands on most issues.

President Donald Trump and top Senate Republicans quickly endorsed Darline Graham to become South Carolina’s next full-term Republican senator. But few Republican lawmakers personally know Graham, who was appointed to the seat just last week.

The low profile could put Graham, a longtime disability advocate who previously served on the South Carolina Commission for the Blind, at a disadvantage, even with Trump’s backing effectively making her the frontrunner in next month’s special election.

“These are people with legislative records that they can point to, that are proven to say, ‘Hey, prices are up, we can bring prices down if we do X, Y and Z. Here’s what I’ve done in the past,’” CJ Westfall, chair of the Dorchester County Republican Party, told NOTUS.

Darline is “somebody that’s unproven and just has the stamp of approval by the president. I don’t think that’s the end-all, be-all for South Carolina,” Westfall added. As a county party chair, he cannot endorse any candidate in the race.

Republican senators are still getting to know Graham, who cast her first votes in the Senate this week after a whirlwind appointment by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster. Initially, many believed she would serve as a caretaker for the last six months of her brother’s term, with several South Carolina Republicans expressing interest in the job, until a surprise Trump endorsement for a full six-year term upended the race.

“She certainly seems competent from the little bit I’ve seen. But competence isn't even a requirement in this job, as I can demonstrate and prove,” Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-North Dakota) joked to NOTUS.

“That’s what primaries are for — to discover those things,” he added. “It’s a very short time frame to prepare. Others who are in the business of politics may have that edge. On the other hand, her answers will be very instructive.”

Graham doesn’t have long to convince South Carolina voters to keep her in Washington. The state will hold a special election on Aug. 11, giving her roughly two weeks to introduce herself to voters after her brother’s funeral plans take place next week. The winner will compete against Democrat Annie Andrews in the November election.

Trump’s endorsement of Graham isn’t scaring off rivals from challenging her. Reps. Ralph Norman and Russell Fry have hopped into the race, along with businessman Mark Lynch. Former Gov. Mark Sanford and Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette are expected to throw their hats in the ring. Evette, notably, came up short in her bid for governor last month despite having Trump’s endorsement, underscoring that Graham’s campaign for Senate is no sure thing.

“Each candidate has a strength,” Tyson Grinstead, chair of the Richland County GOP and a former campaign adviser to Lindsey Graham, told NOTUS. “Darline’s a newcomer but she has Sen. Graham’s campaign and she's got Sen. Graham's structure in place to help her, and so I think that kind of evens out with some of the other candidates.”

“Russell Fry’s definitely got longstanding relationships. Ralph Norman has just come out of the governor’s race,” added Grinstead, who cannot endorse a candidate as a county party chair. “And then you’ve got Darline with Sen. Graham’s campaign, which was one of the only statewide campaigns that had a lot of money spent on it.”

Fry and Norman are pushing for a debate in Charleston on Aug. 4, the day before early voting starts. While the details are still being worked out, Norman suggested that’s where voters will have the opportunity to “find out” more about Graham, who hasn’t yet indicated whether she will participate.

Graham did give a hint about her priorities as senator in a recent interview with Fox News’ Sean Hannity indicating she may focus more on domestic rather than foreign policy.

“I used to see him on the talk shows,” she said of her brother. “I would watch him, and I’d be like, ‘Lindsey, are you just talking about national security all the time?’ And I understand that’s important. Protecting our borders, national security, absolutely. I said, ‘But talk about also what matters to the average person. The price of groceries, the price of gas, health care, insurance, those kind of things.’ That’s what I’m worried about,’” Graham said.

She has moved to quickly align herself with Trump’s key legislative priority, a sweeping bill that would change some voting rules, known as the SAVE America Act. And she has the support of top Senate Republicans who immediately backed her campaign, including Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas, chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee and a staunch defense hawk.

Senate Republicans are also hoping that Graham’s support for a bipartisan Russia sanctions bill, which her brother long advocated for, will help get the legislation across the finish line in Congress and to Trump’s desk.

“Senator Darline Graham has worked for the people of South Carolina for almost 30 years, and now the U.S. Senate is an extension of that service. God calls on ordinary people to do extraordinary things, and it’s clear she has met the moment,” said Taylor Reidy, a Graham spokesperson told NOTUS in a statement.

Touting her work so far, Reidy pointed to her votes to confirm judges and the president’s nominees and added, “Sen. Darline Graham was sworn in eight days ago and in that time alone, she has led the introduction of major sanctions legislation, cosponsored the SAVE America Act and a host of pro-life bills.

Still, policy groups have yet to decide on Graham’s qualifications. Students for Life America, a prominent anti-abortion group, has yet to decide whether it will endorse Graham in the primary, with a spokesperson telling NOTUS on Tuesday that the group is still evaluating her positions. The late senator was an outspoken anti-abortion ally in Congress, and SFLA backed some of his efforts to restrict abortion.

Graham is working quickly to shore up support on the right. On Wednesday, she announced she is co-sponsoring more than a half-dozen anti-abortion rights bills, including the Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection Act.

Despite the questions about her background, Graham does have a number of things working in her favor. Due in large part to her brother and to Trump, she has high name recognition that others running may not enjoy.

“It’s huge statewide. It’ll be low turnout so name recognition will be an even bigger factor,” said Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia), a member of Republican leadership who has endorsed Graham.

One South Carolina Republican strategist who spoke to Graham recently said she wants to chart her own path in the Senate.

“True to Graham fashion, she wants to own her own lane. And it’s not Lindsey’s lane,” the strategist told NOTUS.

Republicans are expecting Graham to begin campaigning in earnest after her brother’s funeral services on July 28. The late senator died at age 71 from a rupture of his aorta due to a hardening of his arteries, according to a preliminary analysis by the D.C. medical examiner.

“I know I’m a hard worker. I learned that from Lindsey,” Graham said in her interview with Hannity. “I feel like I can do it. I feel an inner peace about it. Will it be difficult? Yes. Absolutely.”

Capito conceded that Graham could face a challenge getting her message out in such a short time frame, but indicated she should be able to gather enough financial support.

“I think she will have a challenge getting her own voice out, and I don’t know if that’s a choice she’s going to make,” Capito said. “Is it her own voice, or is it just ‘I’m going to be the voice of my brother’ plus?”

entries.title: Software Vendor Denies Responsibility for New Jersey Voter-Registration Error
entries.summary: IDEMIA, a French company that operates globally, said New Jersey was ultimately responsible for validating and adjudicating voter registrations.
entries.content:
The biometrics and cryptography company that New Jersey officials said was responsible for erroneously adding thousands of noncitizens to voter rolls denied any mishandling — stating that the responsibility of voter registration lies with the state.

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill announced Tuesday that a serious software error caused by IDEMIA, a French company that operates globally, led to roughly 6,600 non-citizens being accidentally registered to vote between June 2023 and June 2024. Fewer than 400 went on to illegally cast ballots, Sherill said, and a preliminary review found that the votes did not sway any elections.

The debacle comes in the middle of intensified debates about election integrity aggravated by President Donald Trump’s widely-debunked assertions that the 2020 election was rigged against him. Trump mentioned the incident during a Wednesday speech in Georgia, falsely stating that “thousands and thousands of votes” were illegally cast.

IDEMIA said in a statement it had worked with the New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission (MVC) for more than 40 years, supporting the system that allows eligible residents to indicate they want to register to vote when they apply for or renew a license or state ID.

“IDEMIA's role is to transmit information through the motor vehicle system,” the statement said, adding that voter registration data is transmitted to the state Division of Elections, which “ultimately” holds responsibility for verification. “Information submitted by IDEMIA must still be validated and adjudicated by the Division of Elections.”

On Wednesday, a Sherrill spokesperson said IDEMIA’s system error could be attributed to the records of people who answered “No” to the citizenship question erroneously being transmitted to the Division of Elections.

IDEMIA refuted the allegations in a statement to NOTUS, saying the 6,600 files submitted to the MVC and Division of Elections contained accurate information “according to the design specifications as set out by the state.” The 6,600 individuals had checked “Yes” to wanting to register to vote and “No” to being a citizen, IDEMIA said.

The files were always available to MVC officials and did not indicate at any point that the individuals were citizens, IDEMIA said. In June 2024, the Division of Elections had alerted the MVC to 6,600 files that were missing a party affiliation, IDEMIA said, but the company did not have confirmation that those individuals were ever registered to vote.

“IDEMIA does not control or manage voter enrollment, our role is simply to collect self-reported citizenship and interest data,” the statement said. “This leads to more questions — if the Division of Elections had missing information which is required to register in the State of New Jersey, did the Division of Elections approve these individuals be added to the Voter Rolls.”

Those who were erroneously registered to vote are being notified by mail and are being removed from the voter rolls, Sherill said on Tuesday. She heavily criticized IDEMIA for releasing software with “such a glaring error,” the MVC for taking more than a year to patch the issue and former Gov. Phil Murphy’s administration for not being transparent about the incident at the time.

Sherrill acknowledged on Tuesday that Trump would likely use the incident to back up his claims of widespread vulnerabilities in the country’s election security system, despite little evidence to support the claim. She said Trump “has zero credibility on the issue of election integrity.”

Noncitizen voting is extremely rare, election officials say, and there is no evidence that it has happened on a scale that could change the results of an election.

The incident has sparked further scrutiny. On Wednesday, Rep. Josh Gottheimer (D-New Jersey) demanded a government-wide audit into IDEMIA’s federal contracts, saying the company handles “an excessive amount of the federal security apparatus.”

“This incident raises serious concerns about the reliability of IDEMIA’s software, the company’s quality control practices, and the federal government’s reliance on a single contractor to manage highly sensitive identity and biometric systems,” Gottheimer wrote in a letter to Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought and U.S. General Services Administration Administrator Edward C. Forst.

entries.title: House Committee Advances Bill Limiting D.C.’s Ability to Raise Taxes
entries.summary: City officials say the measure would “straightjacket” their ability to govern D.C., while DoorDash faces criticism for supporting the bill.
entries.content:
A House committee approved a bill Wednesday that would broadly restrict D.C.’s ability to increase or decrease local taxes and fees, again highlighting Republicans’ aggressive interest in managing how the city runs — down to the dollars and cents it collects.

The bill passed the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform on a party-line vote, sending it next to the full House for consideration. It faces much steeper odds if it gets to the Senate, though.

Speaking during a brief debate, committee Chair James Comer (R-Kentucky), who introduced the measure, said it would benefit residents and businesses and make the city more economically vibrant.

“Radical D.C. Democrats want to solve their spending problem by reaching deeper into taxpayers’ pockets and driving further on the path to socialism,” he said. “Actions like these only serve to hurt small businesses and the District’s already vulnerable residents. These are just more examples of bad policies that disincentivize investment, drive residents out and undermine the economic competitiveness of the city.”

But Comer also conceded that the bill is meant as a preemptive attack on a new class of elected officials who are expected to take office next year, including Ward 4 council member Janeese Lewis George, a democratic socialist who overwhelmingly won the city’s Democratic Party primary in June and is expected to cruise to victory in November’s general election.

“This bill enhances Congress’s constitutional oversight authority over D.C. to restrain irresponsible policies pursued by future socialist and ultra-progressive D.C. Democrats,” he said.

Lewis George has said D.C. should consider raising taxes on certain businesses and wealthy residents to collect new revenue as the city faces a sluggish economy, and the D.C. Council is expected to hold a hearing in the fall on possible revenue-raising options. Comer and other Republicans said Wednesday that city lawmakers should instead focus on cutting spending.

But congressional Democrats and city officials alike pushed back on Comer’s bill, calling it an unnecessary and unwelcome intrusion into plainly local affairs.

“D.C.’s locally elected leaders are accountable to D.C. residents, and local leaders should be empowered to address local matters without congressional interference,” said Rep. Robert Garcia (D-California). “If Donald Trump or congressional Republicans want to run D.C., they should run for mayor and D.C. Council.”

Congress has a significant amount of say in D.C.’s local affairs. Every bill passed by the council undergoes a 30-day review on Capitol Hill (or 60 days when a bill changes criminal law), during which time members of Congress have the power to stop any measure from becoming law. That has happened rarely since D.C. gained home rule more than 50 years ago, though more recently, Republicans have increasingly wielded the power — including a 2023 vote that rejected a sweeping rewrite of the city’s criminal code.

But city officials warned that Comer’s bill would effectively flip the existing process on its head, allowing council bills touching on taxes or fees to become law only if Congress proactively approved them.

“The bill would straightjacket the District because it would paralyze our tax code,” Council Chair Phil Mendelson wrote in a letter to Comer, noting that D.C. Superior Court consistently faces a shortage of judges because confirmation votes are delayed in the Senate.

In her own statement, Mayor Muriel Bowser told Comer — with whom she has otherwise had a friendly relationship — that Congress could take other steps to help the city’s economy, which has been hit by President Donald Trump’s aggressive effort to trim the size of the federal workforce.

“While the federal government should not touch the District's ability to raise and spend its local dollars, they can and should help us replace the economic activity lost through reductions to the federal workforce and a shrinking federal footprint,” she wrote.

Democrats on the House Oversight Committee, including Rep. Maxwell Frost (D-Florida), highlighted what they said was an inherent hypocrisy in the bill: Congress giving itself more responsibility over D.C. while facing persistent challenges passing an annual federal budget.

“We can’t even pass our own bills. Now you want to add to that and pass the bills of D.C.?” Frost asked. “You want to run the D.C. budget? Why don’t we run our own budget?”

While D.C. officials largely criticized Republicans for approving the bill, a second (and unexpected) target also emerged: DoorDash. Comer said during the debate that the food-delivery platform supported his bill, which DoorDash confirmed to NOTUS. John Horton, the platform’s head of North American policy, said its decision was motivated by the council’s recent approval of a 20-cent fee on all third-party deliveries in the city.

"We've said from the start that taxes like this fall hardest on the people D.C. says it wants to protect, and nothing has changed. We have always supported home rule for D.C., but will continue to do everything we can to defend D.C.’s small businesses, local economy, and underserved residents,” Horton wrote in a statement.

DoorDash’s decision prompted outrage from some local advocacy groups, including Free D.C., which called on residents to boycott the app. Ward 5 council member Zachary Parker similarly expressed his anger on social media.

“Every District resident should know that @DoorDash doesn't support DC Home Rule and is actively working to undermine it by lobbying for the GOP’s efforts to control DC tax policies,” he wrote on X. “Govern yourselves accordingly, neighbors.”

entries.title: Second WHCA Dinner Isn't a Security 'Redo' for the Secret Service, Officials Say
entries.summary: Friday’s media dinner was rescheduled after an attack cut the original event short.
entries.content:
Secret Service officials on Wednesday voiced confidence in their security plan for President Donald Trump's visit Friday to the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner, which was rescheduled after a gunman tried to attack the original event in April.

In a rare briefing with reporters at the Secret Service headquarters, Director Sean Curran said officials had sent an advance team of agents to secure the event at the Waldorf Astoria and that they were taking standard steps to prepare.

“We do expect bad people to show up. It’s just the reality of where we are,” Curran said, noting that the dinner was taking place amid a surge in threats against Trump and other protectees. “But we’re treating it no different than any other site that the president goes to.”

Service officials did not provide specifics on their security plans for the event, which the White House Correspondents’ Association said last month would involve “significantly enhanced safety measures and new access procedures.”

Officials said they viewed the thwarted attack on the April dinner as a success. But they emphasized that they didn’t see the rescheduled event as a reprise of security from the first.

“We examine every single site and we change things and get better every single time,” Deputy Director Matthew Quinn said. “We’re not looking at this as a redo of a dinner. We’re looking at this as a presidential site with Cabinet members and other protectees there, just like every other site we do everywhere we go.”

The original dinner, held April 25 at the Washington Hilton, was cut short after an armed man charged through a security checkpoint, firing his weapon and injuring a Secret Service officer before law-enforcement personnel stopped him. Trump and other officials were evacuated while many of the attendees took shelter behind tables and chairs.

The suspect, Cole Tomas Allen, pleaded not guilty in May to charges of attempting to assassinate Trump and weapons violations.

The Secret Service faced scrutiny over its security arrangements at the event, with some lawmakers questioning whether the security perimeter was sufficiently large and raising concerns about how Allen managed to book a room in the hotel. Curran briefed lawmakers privately in the days that followed, but Congress did not hold hearings on the attack.

Speaking with reporters Wednesday, Curran defended the service’s handling of security at the dinner, saying the roughly 120-yard buffer from the magnetometer checkpoint to the podium was adequate.

“How we set up that perimeter and where we ended it is where we felt comfortable, with our special teams, as to where we needed to put it,” Curran said. “We do expect things to happen at the magnetometers, unfortunately. But that’s why they are there. And that’s where it happened, and that’s where it ended. So it did work — the system worked.”

Trump is expected to speak at the rescheduled dinner, which will host fewer attendees than the original. Trump previously owned and operated the Waldorf Astoria building as the Trump International Hotel before his company sold the lease in 2022.

Service officials said that, overall, threats against protectees were running higher than at any point in recent memory. They said the agency’s protective intelligence investigations are up 40% over last year. The increase has strained agents, officers and other staffers, many of whom already work long overtime hours, according to current and former officials.

The shooting at the dinner in April was one of three shootings near the White House in the span of about a month that the Secret Service responded to — the most in recent history for the agency in such a short span. In May, service personnel shot a man who allegedly fired a gun at officers near Vice President JD Vance’s motorcade, and in a separate incident fatally shot a man who opened fire near the White House.

Last month, the Secret Service and FBI said they disrupted a plot to use drones, explosives and snipers to kill politicians and other attendees at the UFC fight held on the White House lawn. At least eight people have been arrested and charged in connection with the alleged plot.

The rescheduled correspondents’ dinner is part of a historically packed schedule of protective events the Secret Service has managed this summer that has included the July 4 fireworks celebration and other festivities around America’s 250th anniversary.

entries.title: Trump Offered Gold Star Family a Ride on His New Air Force One
entries.summary: The family of the late Lt. Tyler Feehan rode with the president from Dover Air Force Base to a rally in Georgia.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump said he offered to give Gold Star family members a ride on his newly outfitted Air Force One Wednesday following a dignified transfer ceremony to honor fallen service members.

He revealed the gesture at a campaign rally in Georgia, where he appeared with Republican gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson and Rep. Mike Collins, who is running for Senate. The family of Lt. Tyler Feehan, 25, appears to have taken him up on the offer.

“I said, ‘So if you want, I’ll give you a ride on Air Force One. And they said, ‘Wow,’” Trump recalled during his remarks, adding of the plane: “It’s quite nice, I must say.”

Trump also thanked Feehan’s family by name, saying that he was impressed by the young soldier’s sterling record. Feehan died in an Iranian attack on his base in Jordan last weekend.

“To Sherry and Stephen and David, we will carry Tyler’s memory in our hearts forever, and I just want to thank you. It’s an honor to have you here today,” the president said, gesturing to the family.

Also at the rally, Trump said attending the dignified transfer is the “toughest thing” he has done as president.

Dignified Transfers take place at the Dover Air Force Base in Delaware, where U.S. service member's remains are transferred from an arriving aircraft to a transport vehicle, ensuring fallen troops are honored and that their bodies are handled with dignity.

On Wednesday, the remains of four soldiers killed in the Iran war were brought back to American soil and honored. Those soldiers were Feehan; Pvt. Isabella Gonzalez, 19; Sgt. Michael Emmanuel Swinton, 30; and Sgt. Angel Rampersad, 28.

Following the ceremony, Trump said he spoke with Feehan’s family and discovered that they were from Georgia — which prompted him to offer them a ride on his new jet and an opportunity to see his rally.

The new Air Force One that Trump has been using for domestic flights — including Wednesday’s trip — was gifted to him from Qatar, and is set to be donated to Trump’s presidential library after he leaves office. Renovations to the luxury jet, including many security upgrades, cost approximately $400 million in taxpayer funds.

The jet is intended as a “bridge” between the aging Boeing jets used by previous presidents and two new aircrafts currently under construction. Those jets are years behind schedule and are due to be delivered in 2028 at the earliest.

Trump took the upgraded Air Force One on its maiden voyage earlier this month on a trip to Turkey to attend a NATO summit, but did not ride the plane back to the U.S. due to widely reported security concerns.

News stories outlining the aircraft’s security vulnerabilities led the Justice Department to serve a series of highly unusual subpoenas toNew York Times reporters and their relatives in an attempt to unmask the confidential sources who spoke with the newspaper.

One reporter’s mother was even targeted by the administration, according to the Times.
